description: We are students passionate about space exploration, science, and innovation. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we aim to develop AnalogLab, a tool using open NASA data to identify and compare potential Earth analogs for Mars exploration. Our team combines research, programming, design, and communication. We value teamwork and seek strengths in Earth science, data analysis, GIS, and web development.
summary: MISSION 30 is a turn-based educational simulator that lets players ages 10 to 16 train as mission planners. Players have 30 days to fly from Earth to the Moon, run a lunar base, travel on to Mars, and set up a science outpost, all without running out of oxygen, energy, water, or food. Each day, players choose which life support systems to run, how many food rations to use, and what task the astronaut performs. A daily report explains why every number changed, and a Compare Plans tool lets players test two options before spending any resources. Daily consumption values for oxygen, food, and water are based on NASA data, while other mechanics are simplified for gameplay. The game responds to the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning real life support trade-offs into short, replayable decisions. It runs in any web browser, works offline after the first visit, and collects no personal data.
details:
MISSION 30 is a turn-based simulator where each turn is one mission day, and players have 30 days to complete a journey from Earth to the Moon and on to Mars. There is no real-time clock, so players can think through each decision. Each day, players check four indicators (oxygen, energy, water, and food), choose which life support systems to run (oxygen generator, water recycler, greenhouse), set the number of food rations, and assign a task to the astronaut, such as repairing equipment, resting, building, or going on a spacewalk. Every choice spends resources, and a daily report explains why each number changed.

The mission has four phases: the Earth to Moon transit, the lunar south pole base, the Moon to Mars transit, and the Mars base. Each phase has its own challenge, such as a meteorite damaging the oxygen pump, lunar shadow days that cut solar power, a solar alert during the trip to Mars, and dust storms on Mars. Players win by building the habitat, utilities, and greenhouse, installing a science station, and transmitting data while keeping oxygen, nutrition, and hygiene above 50%. They lose if oxygen, health, energy, or drinking water runs out. A defeat screen explains what happened with real numbers, and players can retry the previous day.

In-game radio messages from three crewmates, a “Why?” button, sunlight forecasts, alerts, and a mission log help players connect cause and effect. The goal is for students ages 10 to 16 to learn systems thinking, resource management, and planning under pressure through consequences instead of dense text.

We used official data provided by NASA as the scientific basis for the game. Other mechanics are simplified for gameplay, and we kept the two clearly separate. The project does not claim NASA endorsement.

Creative choices include our own pixel-art style, custom icons, a 30-day mission clock, and an original “M30” mission patch.

> Technical details: TypeScript, HTML and CSS for the web game, with a deterministic rules engine. Python scripts prepare assets and check sources; GDScript (Godot) and C# (Unity) renderer sources are included but not compiled. The game is a static web app of about 2.1 MB with no server, no accounts and no personal data. It works offline after the first visit and on phones and tablets (tested by emulation). Accessibility: screen-reader labels, full keyboard control, high contrast and 44 px touch targets. 250 unit tests and 179 browser checks run automatically. Development used AI assistants for ideation, research, coding and debugging; design decisions and testing were reviewed by the team.
